name: Guardian cryptic crossword, Penguin book 5 No 44

book.title: The New Penguin Book of The Guardian Crosswords, volume 5

entries.clue: Polish image for historic crossing (7)

blocks.note: to polish a table is to rub it
an icon is a painted image of a saint, and the word now covers any little image on a screen

annotation.surface: Someone buffing up a picture of a famous frontier.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital P on the first word is the trap: it wants to be the nation and is only the verb, which the start of a clue licenses. Caesar took his army over in 49 BC against the Senate's orders.
annotation.definitionFit: The Rubicon is the small Italian stream Caesar led his legions across, and that act is the crossing history remembers.

entries.clue: Milton’s friend lays off entertaining detectives (7)

indicatorNotes.off: Milk that has gone off is no longer what it was, and letters told they are off come out in another order.
indicatorNotes.entertaining: To entertain visitors is to have them in the house, so the word doing the entertaining opens up and takes the next letters inside.

blocks.note: four letters to be re-set
the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the plain-clothes branch of a British police force

annotation.surface: A poet sacking staff while keeping the detectives amused.
annotation.walkthrough: Milton's elegy of 1637 mourns Edward King, a Cambridge contemporary drowned in the Irish Sea, under a shepherd's name borrowed from Greek pastoral. 'Lays' are songs as well as a sacking, which is the surface's second joke.
annotation.definitionFit: Lycidas is the pastoral name Milton gave the drowned companion he lamented, so the poem's title stands for the friend himself.

entries.clue: Queen enters Cornish river in the wild (5)

indicatorNotes.enters: A guest who enters a house is inside it once through the door, so the letters before the word go in between the letters after it.

blocks.note: the Fal runs down through Cornwall to the harbour of Falmouth, which takes its name from it
Elizabeth Regina signed herself ER, and those two letters are the crossword's standing queen

annotation.surface: The monarch wading into a Cornish river somewhere out in open country.
annotation.walkthrough: Cornwall's short rivers — the Fal, the Fowey, the Camel — are a setter's stock of three- and five-letter fillers, and the Fal is the one that keeps turning up. ER comes from the royal cypher on a postbox.
annotation.definitionFit: A cat that has gone back to living rough, generations away from any owner, is called feral, so the phrase names the state exactly.

entries.clue: Unnatural verdict on crash (9)

indicatorNotes.crash: A crash leaves the pieces of a thing lying in no particular order, which is what happens to the letters in front of it.

blocks.note: nine letters to be re-set, exactly the length wanted

annotation.surface: A coroner's finding delivered on a road smash.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' looks like the word joining the verdict to the crash and is really two of the nine letters. Setters like 'crash' because it can shuffle a word while still reading as part of the story.
annotation.definitionFit: Something contrived has been deliberately worked up rather than arising of itself, which is what calling it unnatural says of it.

entries.clue: Most of those who ‘come to dust’ permit a summer visitor (7-7)

indicatorNotes.Most of: Most of a thing is the greater part of it and not all of it, so what is named next keeps its opening letters and gives up the tail.

blocks.note: the song in Cymbeline has golden lads and girls, as chimney-sweepers, come to dust; nine of those fifteen letters are kept
to permit a thing is to allow it

annotation.surface: Those destined for the grave are granted a guest for the summer.
annotation.walkthrough: The quoted words are from the funeral song in Cymbeline — 'Golden lads and girls all must, as chimney-sweepers, come to dust' — so the people meant are sweeps. Quotation marks in a clue flag borrowed words rather than wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: The chimney swallow is the barn swallow of British eaves and chimneys, in from Africa by April and gone again in October.

entries.clue: Knocked back a bit of gin (4)

indicatorNotes.Knocked back: What is knocked back is sent the way it came, so the letters run right to left across the grid.

blocks.note: a bit of something is a part of it, and those four letters are set down from the back

annotation.surface: Somebody tossing back a small measure of gin.
annotation.walkthrough: The gin is not the drink but the wire snare a poacher sets, a word that survives mostly in gin trap. 'Knocked back' does both jobs at once: swallowing the measure and writing the letters backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A gin is the sprung snare set in a hedge for rabbits, so it is a trap in the oldest sense the word has.

entries.clue: What turned brass instrument to wood? (8)

indicatorNotes.turned: Milk that has turned is not what it was, and a word told it has turned comes out with its letters in a new order.

blocks.note: the clue's opening word is four letters to be re-set
the horn is the brass section's own instrument

annotation.surface: A baffled question about the alchemy that made a brass instrument wooden.
annotation.walkthrough: The opening word poses the question and is also the fodder, which is what the question mark is really apologising for. Hawthorn is the may tree of English hedgerows, and its timber is white, close-grained and very hard.
annotation.definitionFit: Hawthorn is the hedgerow tree whose hard pale timber was cut for tool handles and mallets, so its name serves for the wood as well as the tree.

entries.clue: Blame agent for fish (8)

blocks.note: the shortening the sales trade uses for its representatives
a small silver fish of English rivers and canals

annotation.surface: Blaming the travelling salesman for the state of the fish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Blame' works as noun and verb, and the answer is the verb — what you do, not what is done. Nothing in the clue marks the join: two words set end to end is the oldest charade shape there is.
annotation.definitionFit: To reproach someone is to tell them off for a fault, which is blaming them to their face.

entries.clue: Palindromic being could follow fin (4)

indicatorNotes.Palindromic: A palindromic word reads the same from either end, so whatever goes in here has to survive being spelt backwards.

blocks.note: the word those three letters begin is finesse, and taking them off the front leaves four

annotation.walkthrough: Esse is the Latin infinitive 'to be', kept in English philosophy for existence itself: a thing in esse actually is, as against a thing in posse, which only might be. The mirror-reading is a free check on the fill.
annotation.definitionFit: Esse is the Latin 'to be' borrowed whole into philosophy for existence itself, which is what is meant by a being.

entries.clue: Third and last repeat left eggs in shadow of former European country (14)

indicatorNotes.in: Letters put in something end up surrounded by it, so what comes before the word drops inside what comes after.

blocks.note: the third letter of the alphabet and the last one, in that order
a shout repeated back off a hillside is an echo
skia is the Greek for shadow, the skia- of skiagraphy, drawing in shadow
L is the standard shortening of left, as stamped in a boot
ova is the plural of the Latin ovum, an egg

annotation.surface: Somebody repeating an order for the third and last time and leaving eggs in the shade.
annotation.walkthrough: Two of the letters come straight out of the alphabet, its third and its last, and a word of Greek does the rest of the work. Czechoslovakia split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia at midnight on the last day of 1992.
annotation.definitionFit: Czechoslovakia was the state founded in 1918 between Germany and Ukraine, and it divided in two at the end of 1992, so it is European and gone.

entries.clue: Theatrical agency? (9)

blocks.note: read as belonging to the stage, and meant as belonging to the theatre a surgeon works in
read as a firm that acts for you, and meant as plain action — the agency of a drug is what it does

annotation.surface: A firm that finds work for actors.
annotation.walkthrough: The theatre is the surgeon's rather than the stage's, so that first word carries the whole joke. 'Agency' is a dictionary sense of the answer: the operation of a law is the way it works on people.
annotation.definitionFit: An operation is agency in the plain sense — a thing in operation is at work — and a surgical one is performed in a theatre, which makes it theatrical.

entries.clue: Wrinkles on your head, one more than eight? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: One more than eight is nine, and the answer is not a number: the definition works through the idiom 'one over the eight', which is what a drinker has had when the ninth goes down.

indicatorNotes.head: A word's head is its front, so only the opening letter of the word before it is wanted.

blocks.note: a wrinkle is a handy hint or dodge, the kind one passes on quietly
the front letter of 'your'

annotation.surface: Lines forming on your forehead as the ninth drink goes down.
annotation.walkthrough: A wrinkle in older English is a useful hint, and that is the sense wanted rather than the lines on a forehead. 'One over the eight' is British for one drink past steadiness, eight pints being the notional ration.
annotation.definitionFit: 'One over the eight' is the old British phrase for having had a drink too many, and the person it describes is unsteady rather than properly drunk.

entries.clue: End of cold war sees canvas in river (7)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in a thing sits inside it, so the letters named before the word are planted in the middle of the word after.

blocks.note: the Dee runs out at Aberdeen and another at Chester, and three letters make it a setter's favourite
the canvas you sleep under on a hillside

annotation.surface: The cold war ending while a tent floats down a river.
annotation.walkthrough: Détente is French for a slackening — the same word covers the easing of a trigger spring — and it named the thaw between Washington and Moscow in the 1970s. 'Sees' does nothing but join the two halves.
annotation.definitionFit: Détente is the easing of hostility between two armed powers, and it is by that thaw rather than by fighting that a cold war comes to a close.

entries.clue: Inversion of bureaucracy coming to a point (7)

indicatorNotes.Inversion: An inversion turns a thing the other way up, so the two halves of the phrase change places and the back one arrives first.

blocks.note: the clogging paperwork of officialdom is red tape, whose second word leads off here
the colour word of that same phrase, now bringing up the rear

annotation.surface: Officialdom stood on its head and finally getting to the point.
annotation.walkthrough: Red tape is the pink ribbon that once tied legal papers into bundles, and turning the phrase end for end is the whole instruction. 'Coming to a point' describes a shape here, not an argument reaching its conclusion.
annotation.definitionFit: A tapered spire or table leg narrows steadily along its length until it finishes in a point.

entries.clue: Flat boat called George (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half does not describe the word, it names a man: George Raft, the Hollywood gangster actor of the 1930s, so 'called George' points at a surname rather than a meaning.

blocks.note: the platform of lashed logs you pole across a river on
the surname of the coin-flipping film gangster whose first name that is

annotation.surface: A flat-bottomed boat that somebody has given a name to.
annotation.walkthrough: George Raft played the gangsters Cagney and Robinson left over, and ended up as the millionaire in Some Like It Hot. Boats really are named, so the second half reads as plain surface, which is where the clue hides.
annotation.definitionFit: A raft is the flat platform of lashed timber that floats without a hull, and Raft was the surname of the film actor whose first name was George.

entries.clue: Third form at a World War I battle scene in crooked annual offering (8,7)

indicatorNotes.form: To form something is to shape it out of what you have, so the letters before the word are made into a new shape.
indicatorNotes.in: What goes in a word is held inside it, so everything named before the word is planted in the middle of what follows.

blocks.note: a crooked official is a bent one, and these four letters open to take the rest
five letters to be re-set
the article, taken as it stands
Ypres is the Flemish town where the British held the line through three of the war's worst battles

annotation.surface: A third-form class on a school trip to a Great War battlefield.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Third form' is a school year in the story and five shuffled letters in the wordplay, which is why the class had to be that one. The troops could not manage the Flemish name and called the town Wipers.
annotation.definitionFit: A birthday present is the gift that comes round once a year for the same person, which is what an annual offering is.

entries.clue: Pillar of the press? (6)

blocks.note: the upright stone shaft that holds a portico up
a newspaper page divides into vertical strips, and a regular writer is given one to fill

annotation.surface: A grand old figure of the newspaper world.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pillar of' normally introduces a person — a pillar of the community — and the question mark is the setter quietly withdrawing that. A newspaper page is still set in vertical strips, which is what the writer's weekly piece is named after.
annotation.definitionFit: A column is both the stone upright of a temple front and the strip of newsprint a regular contributor fills, so the press has pillars in two senses at once.

entries.clue: Coin for constabulary and railway (6)

blocks.note: the nick is British slang for the police station, and so for the police themselves
the El is the elevated railway that runs above the streets of Chicago and once of New York

annotation.surface: Paying off the police and the trains in small change.
annotation.walkthrough: The coin is the United States five-cent piece, struck from a copper-nickel alloy that gave it the name. 'Constabulary' keeps the first half on the right side of the law, since nick is just as often the verb for stealing.
annotation.definitionFit: A nickel is the American five-cent piece, named for the metal it was first struck from.

entries.clue: Covers inside of island to help referee (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a person and the phrase reads as an instruction; 'help' is being used as the noun for one who assists, the way a hired help is a person, so the two words name the referee's assistant.

blocks.note: to line a coat or a box is to cover it on the inside
the Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea, and setters reach for it whenever an island has to be three letters

annotation.surface: Sheeting laid over the middle of an island so the referee gets some help.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Covers' looks like a noun — blankets, or fielding positions — and is the verb to line. The linesman ran the touchline with a flag until football renamed him the assistant referee, though the older word holds on in other sports.
annotation.definitionFit: A linesman patrols the touchline and flags what the referee cannot see from the middle, which makes him the referee's help.

entries.clue: Hot stuff about insect being full of fruit (8)

indicatorNotes.about: Something set about a thing is wrapped right round it, so the word before opens up and the word after drops inside.

blocks.note: the dish that comes to the table hot enough to need a lager with it
the ant is the crossword's standing insect, three letters and always at work

annotation.surface: Warm gossip about an insect that has been at the fruit bowl.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hot stuff' is the dish rather than the gossip the surface offers. Curranty is the old kitchen adjective for a loaf or a bun with plenty of currants through it — currants being the dried grapes of a Christmas pudding.
annotation.definitionFit: A curranty bun or tea loaf is one baked with currants all the way through it, which is what being full of that fruit amounts to.

entries.clue: Satanist or corrupt liver who’s taken in by Baptist? (5-10)

indicatorNotes.corrupt: A corrupt text is one whose letters have been garbled in the copying, so the words after it come out in a different order.
indicatorNotes.taken in by: To be taken in by someone is to be swallowed whole by them, so these letters end up inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: Baptists baptise by full immersion, which earned them the old nickname of dippers
nine letters to be re-set, the apostrophe ignored as always

annotation.surface: A Satanist, or else some man of bad life taken in by a Baptist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Liver' is not the organ but one who lives: an evil liver is a person of bad life, an old phrase the surface leans on. The question mark admits that 'dipper' is a nickname for a Baptist rather than a definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Satan is the devil of Christian tradition, so the man who worships him and the Satanist are one and the same, named from either side.

entries.clue: Breeze from the beam returned with snake or missile (10)

indicatorNotes.from: 'From' names where the breeze starts out, and a wind is always named for the quarter it blows from, so that quarter is written first.

blocks.note: a ship's beam is its widest part athwartships, so anything on the beam lies off to one side
a breeze is a light wind
read the word as re-turned: the two letters that usually mean 'about' set down the other way round

annotation.surface: A wind off the beam coming back, with a snake or a missile for company.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Returned' is the cleverest word in the clue, hiding a two-letter reversal inside an ordinary participle. A vessel's beam is its side, so a breeze from the beam is one blowing square across the course rather than along it.
annotation.definitionFit: A sidewinder is the desert rattlesnake that flings itself sideways over loose sand, and also the heat-seeking missile named after it.

entries.clue: Scene of disturbance conveyed by doctor to locums (5-5)

indicatorNotes.conveyed: What is conveyed is carried from one place to another, and letters carried about end up standing in new positions.

blocks.note: the two letters on a surgery nameplate
eight letters taken as they stand, joined to the two in front

annotation.surface: A note the doctor passes to the stand-in about where the trouble is.
annotation.walkthrough: A locum is the substitute doctor who covers a practice while its own is away, which is what makes the surface read as a handover. 'Doctor' is fodder here, not the anagram indicator it usually is — the shuffling word is 'conveyed'.
annotation.definitionFit: A storm-cloud is the black mass a squall builds itself in, so it is where the weather's disturbance is visibly gathering.

entries.clue: Receive information about Scottish interjection in Scottish water (4,4)

indicatorNotes.about: Something placed about a thing is wrapped round it, so the words before it open to take the next lot inside.

blocks.note: to receive information is to learn it
och is the Scots exclamation of impatience or regret — och aye, och well

annotation.surface: Picking up a bit of news about a Scots exclamation made by the water.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scottish' does two different jobs in one clue: first the exclamation, then the country the water is in. Loch Earn is the seven-mile loch in Perthshire with St Fillans at one end and Lochearnhead at the other.
annotation.definitionFit: Loch Earn is a long freshwater loch in Perthshire, and loch is simply the Scots word for a lake.

entries.clue: Scottish isles with some silent are soon split (8)

indicatorNotes.some: 'Some' asks for a part of the word that follows rather than the whole of it, so its closing letters are dropped and what is in front of them kept.

blocks.note: Sc. is the dictionary's label on a Scots word
Is. is how an atlas shortens isles or islands
the first four letters of the word, its last two left behind

annotation.surface: Quiet Scottish islands that do not stay in one piece for long.
annotation.walkthrough: Both shortenings are map-and-dictionary stock: Sc. for Scottish, Is. for isles. Scissile is the mineralogist's word for a crystal that cleaves cleanly, and it shares its Latin root with scissors.
annotation.definitionFit: Something scissile cleaves readily along its grain, so it comes apart as soon as a blade is put to it.

entries.clue: Instrument formerly commissioned (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The second definition names a rank instead of describing a thing: the cornet was the junior commissioned officer of a British cavalry troop, and 'formerly' marks the sense as one no army uses now.

blocks.note: the small brass horn of the town band, shorter and mellower than a trumpet
the lowest commissioned rank in a cavalry regiment, the officer who carried the troop's colours

annotation.surface: A piece of equipment that somebody ordered a long time ago.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Commissioned' reads as a thing ordered from a maker and means an officer's commission instead. The rank went in 1871, when Cardwell's reforms abolished both it and the practice of buying a commission outright.
annotation.definitionFit: A cornet is the compact brass instrument of the brass band, and a cornet was also the cavalry's most junior commissioned officer until the rank was abolished.

entries.clue: Northern European gets round to portable computer (3-3)

indicatorNotes.gets round: To get round something is to pass all the way about it, so the word before closes round the word after.

blocks.note: a Lapp is a member of the Sami people of northern Scandinavia, under the older name the dictionaries still carry
the word itself, worth two letters

annotation.surface: A Scandinavian finally getting round to his portable computer.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gets round to' reads as a single phrase meaning to do a thing at last, and the clue means the middle word of it literally. Lapp is the old name for the Sami, now avoided in Norway and Sweden in favour of their own.
annotation.definitionFit: A lap-top is the computer built small enough to work on your knees, which is what makes it the portable kind.

entries.clue: Composer who sounds like singer of air (4)

indicatorNotes.sounds like: 'Sounds like' asks for the noise a word makes rather than its spelling, so what follows is to be heard and then written another way.

blocks.note: the creature that sings up in the air is a bird, and said aloud it is a surname

annotation.surface: A composer whose name is said the same way as a creature singing in the sky.
annotation.walkthrough: An air is a tune as well as the sky, so the singer of airs and the singer in the air come to the same creature. William Byrd wrote masses for recusant Catholics while holding a post in Elizabeth's own chapel.
annotation.definitionFit: William Byrd wrote the masses, motets and virginal music of the Elizabethan court, which puts him among the great English composers.
